Korean-Style Grilled Duck Breast

Chapter 01 / 20 meat recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: contemporary. Duck is the guest at this table, not a native — you will not find it on the old grill lists — but the Korean pantry fits it like it was invited: duck's rich fat wants sesame, soy, garlic, and ginger, and the sharp fresh banchan cut it exactly where it needs cutting. This record runs a skin-on breast the French way, cross-hatched and rendered slow, then finished in the Korean register with a soy-ginger brush and a scallion-sesame finish. Written honestly: a modern bridge, and a good one.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Score the fat, not the meat. Crosshatch the skin at 5 mm intervals, shallow — the blade should never reach the pink. The grid gives the fat somewhere to render from and crisps in diamonds.
  • Salt the skin and rest 30 minutes, refrigerated, uncovered. Dry skin is crisp skin; this half hour matters more than any marinade on this record.
  • Whisk the brush sauce and set it at the grill station.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Cold pan, skin down. The one instruction that sounds wrong and is right: the breast goes into a cold pan or onto a grill grate set at its lowest, skin down, and the heat comes up under it. Render 8–10 minutes at gentle heat, pouring off the fat as it pools (keep it — duck fat is this record's second product). Checkpoint — the skin should go from pale to deep gold slowly, the crosshatch opening as the fat renders out of it. No spitting violence: if the pan roars, the heat is too high and the skin browns before the fat has left — lower it and pour off the fat.
  2. 02
    Flip to the flesh side, 2–3 minutes only, brushing the cooked flesh face with the sauce as it comes off the heat. Duck breast's doneness is medium — the center rosy at 54–56 °C on a thermometer, or the feel of the base of your thumb when your thumb touches your ring finger. Checkpoint — the flesh face should be just colored and glazed, not crusted. Overcooked duck is the record's only real failure; a rosy center is correct here in a way it never is for chicken (#M16, #M17) — duck is served medium at every table that knows it.
  3. 03
    Rest 8 minutes — the full eight. Duck carries hard, and a breast cut at the pan bleeds its juice onto the board; a breast cut at eight keeps it. Then slice across the breast, on the bias, into thick coins, skin up. Sesame and scallion over, the rest of the brush sauce spooned around. Checkpoint — eating test, with the sharp salad in the same bite: crisp, fully rendered skin; rosy, silky-fatty flesh; soy-ginger glaze; then the geotjeori's vinegar cutting clean. Rich, then reset — that rhythm is the whole plate. Chef’s Note — the rendered fat you poured off is half the yield: keep it in a jar in the fridge and cook the next week's potatoes or the breakfast eggs in it. And a note for the tabletop purists — yes, this is a solo-stove record rather than a brazier record, and it sits on this site because of the pantry, not the fire: duck rewards the jang set so well that it has earned a seat at the table even without old papers. Serve it sliced at the center of the table like any other gui, and nobody will ask for its documents.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Skin flabby, fat under itHeat too high too earlyCold pan start, gentle heat, pour off fat
Gray, dry meatCooked to chicken's ruleMedium is correct: 54–56 °C, rosy center
Juice flooded the boardNo restThe full 8 minutes
Skin stuck at the startMoved too soonThe skin releases as it renders; patience

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Raw breasts salted keep 24 hours. Cooked, 3 days sliced — cold duck coins over rice with the sauce, or a ssam with perilla and a swipe of ssamjang (#SA01) where the fusion lane lives.
  • Variations: a gochujang-honey brush for the spicy fork; the same treatment on duck legs runs twice the render time; the reserved fat in place of sesame oil in the scallion dip (#SA04).
